threads.title: [grug] Add the Hero H100 pipeline prototype
threads.body:
Add a separate `experiments/grug/moe_hero_pipeline` variant with stage-local Hero pipeline initialization, weighted loss and quantile-balancing (QB) router updates, host activation/optimizer offloading, and a bounded synthetic runner. The adapter imports the existing `moe_hero_ep` model and optimizer components and defaults to standard 1F1B. Its runner and usage documentation live with the pipeline variant. The adapter uses the current shared router-stat reducer and a size-one context mesh axis required by Hero parameter shardings. CPU tests compare staged hidden states, router statistics, losses, and gradients with the unsplit model.

The full 535B model completed ten finite 65K-context updates on 192 H100s at PP24/EP8, batch 384, with 15.523% median MFU. Those measurements used local JAXPP overlays; the documented command is not yet reproducible with the stock dependency pin. This draft remains blocked on memory-space/host-residual fixes and an explicit startup-preparation API, including the runner's precompile_pipeline_tasks dependency. The Muon expert-stack sharding fix (#9278) has merged into main. Production checkpoint continuation and long-run stability are unvalidated.

The cleaned runner retains the per-step CUDA completion workaround for intermittent NaNs; the cause of the intermittent NaNs remains unresolved. Diagnostic telemetry was removed after the hardware measurements, so the cleaned runner has no new hardware performance claim. DualPipeV-only dependency overlays remain outside this change.

After merging main at 06da233d9a, all seven focused pipeline tests passed with unchanged numerical tolerances. The affected safe suite finished with 2,156 passing tests and eight macOS loopback-interface failures. All eight failures reproduced independently on that main revision. Required lint, project-wide types, and documentation links passed. GPU validation was not rerun after moving the adapter into its separate variant or updating the base. Part of #9277.

threads.title: [deps] Match the pipeline FA4 stack to Levanter's GPU pins
threads.body:
The root pipeline extra still allowed flash-attn-4 4.0.0b16, CUTLASS DSL 4.6.0 and QuACK 0.6.1, while levanter[gpu] requires flash-attn-4 >=4.0.0b27, CUTLASS DSL 4.6.2 and QuACK 0.6.4, and Marin's FA4 adapters call the newer preprocess and postprocess signatures. Use Levanter's pins in the pipeline extra; the lock resolves flash-attn-4 to 4.0.0b28. JAX stays at 0.11.0 for JaxPP.

With these pins, FA4's unpinned Torch import resolves standalone levanter[gpu] installs to a CUDA Torch 2.10.0 from PyPI. A flat CPU-Torch fallback index keeps those installs on CPU Torch; marin-core[gpu] still selects its CUDA Torch index explicitly.

The same versions (flash-attn-4 4.0.0b28, CUTLASS DSL 4.6.2, QuACK 0.6.4, JAX 0.11.0) have run under JaxPP on H100 in the context-parallel integration (#9283, results in #9277): an eight-layer PP4/EP4/CP2 pipeline completed ten updates on 32 H100s, and the full 535B model completed ten updates on 192 H100s. Those runs also used scratch JaxPP overlays, and the environment built from this lock has not itself been run on GPU.

threads.title: [fast-track] Marin Belay v1: hill-climb the scaling ladder (Paloma macro loss, 8 min on 8×H100)
threads.body:
This issue tracks iterative improvements to the Marin pretraining scaling ladder (`experiments/grug/fast_track`) using the **Marin Belay** process. It is a twist on autoresearch: an agent runs experiments in batches, and anyone can steer it with research directions. > **To suggest a research direction, comment on [Marin Belay Intake (#9514)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514).** Suggestions a maintainer approves (👍 from a `marin-devs` member) are copied into this thread automatically, and the agent acts only on this thread. This thread holds the agent's batch reports and maintainer steering. ![fast_track MoE ladder: Marin 535B baseline, clean KMA and candidate 9](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/9697c11ef215ec0f9d536a1bceb0876f768fcf26/v1/ladder_scaling.png) The Marin 535B compute-optimal baseline follows `L(C) = 1.2 + 59.0·C^(−0.0843)` over four data-matched rungs. Clean KMA, the current baseline (★), is 0.022 lower at d512, 0.049 lower at d768, 0.040 lower at d1024 and 0.033 lower at d1280, which is about 1.14×, 1.43×, 1.40× and 1.35× the baseline's compute efficiency. Its dashed curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 64.8·C^(−0.0870)`. The **?** marks the open question this issue is chasing: how much further down each point can go. The red diamonds are the current best recipe, candidate 9 (Status below): **2.977 / 2.725 / 2.515 / 2.397** at d512 / d768 / d1024 / d1280. d512 and d768 are seed means, and the bigram table follows rule A. d768–d1280 are data-matched; d512 sits at its fixed-time step count (2817 vs 2383 steps), so it's plotted slightly to the right. That is 0.157 / 0.098 / 0.078 / 0.074 below clean KMA. Its dash-dot curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 55.0·C^(−0.0847)`. Its slope is a little shallower than clean KMA's, so the gap narrows with compute: projected to **1e24 FLOPs, 1.710 vs clean KMA's 1.727, about 1.48× clean KMA's compute efficiency and 2.95× the 535B baseline's**. Because the fixed-time d512 point flattens the fitted slope, that projection is probably conservative. The right panel is clean KMA's training MFU at each rung on one 8×H100 node: 9.5% at d512 and d768, 12.2% at d1024, and 13.0% at d1280. FLOPs are counted from KMA's own layers (KDA, MLA + Inkling, AttnRes), as 3× forward with no recompute. The trainer's logged `throughput/mfu` uses the baseline architecture's FLOP formula, so it is slightly off for KMA. ## Objective **Minimize Paloma macro loss (`eval/paloma/macro_loss`, final step) at the d512 rung after a fixed 8 minutes of 8×H100 train-step time.** - **Fixed time, not fixed tokens.** Faster code trains on more tokens within the 8 minutes, so a pure speedup counts as a win. - The LR schedule depends on the step count, so fix steps before each run: `num_steps = round(480 s × ex/s ÷ batch)`. - Measure ex/s with a short `--no-eval` probe (~30 steps) on the same cluster, and use the steady-state throughput. - Compile, evals and startup are excluded from the 8 minutes. - **Numerics changes are allowed** (e.g. FP8, precision changes, approximate kernels). They count as ordinary wins; no parity check needed. - **Noise.** Differences under ~0.005 are noise. A win must beat the current best by more than 0.005. ### Gates (both relative to the current baseline, same fixed-time rule at each rung) - **Gate 1:** beat the baseline at d512 and d768. - **Gate 2:** also beat it at d1024 and d1280, **and** project to lower Paloma macro loss at 1e24 FLOPs. Fit a power law of final loss against training FLOPs across the four rungs, for both the baseline and the variant, fixing the asymptote to 1.2. ### Fixed - Training data, the 16k BPE tokenizer, and the eval sets. - Sequence length 4096. - One 8×H100 node per rung. - The FLOP accounting used for the gate-2 projection. ### Judgment calls - **Hero-scale speed is out of scope for v1, so use discretion.** - Robust target criteria would also check training speed and inference speed at hero scale. Marin Belay v1 skips those checks. - Judge whether a change's d512 gain would carry over to hero scale, and avoid changes whose gain comes from d512-only effects. Two examples: - Dropping MoE for dense would be a clear win at d512 because dense gets ~5× higher MFU there, but that MFU gain would not carry over at hero scale. - A much larger KV cache would also be a clear win at d512, but it would hurt long-context inference speed. - **Avoid magic numbers.** - Prefer changes with few new tuned constants. A tuned constant is justified when its gain is above the noise threshold and holds as a pattern across scales. For example, a 2× LR on one parameter group qualifies if it clears the noise threshold and the gain shows up consistently at larger rungs. - The higher a change's risk of curve fitting, the more scales it must be validated at before it counts as a win. - **Spend effort in proportion to an idea's likelihood of improvement.** - Promising ideas deserve several attempts. Long shots can be tried once and dropped. - A first run is not a verdict for a large change. If you try a new architecture or component, tune its optimizer assignment, LR, init and other key hyperparameters before concluding it doesn't work. The baseline's settings were tuned for the baseline, not for the new idea. ## Architecture (current best, d512) The diagrams below show **clean KMA**. The current best recipe adds the components listed under **Status → Current best recipe**: MLA key norm and key offset, a gated bigram-memory AttnRes source, ReLU² experts, and optimizer, schedule and logit changes. The diagrams show d512; the other rungs differ in the Shape table only. **1. Layer stack and Block Attention Residuals.** Every sublayer reads its input through its own AttnRes gate, a per-token softmax over the residual history. At d512 and d768 every layer closes a block. At d1024 (12 layers) and d1280 (14 layers) only layers 0–7 do, so layers 8 and up all accumulate into one running partial instead of their own blocks. **Optimizer routing:** - **MuonH:** every attention and MoE matrix, and every GatedNorm (KDA `W_β` at 2× the MuonH LR). - **AdamH:** lm_head. - **Adam:** embedding, router, attention output gate, norm gains, ShortConv kernels, KDA decay parameters, Inkling weights. - **Adam at 0.1× the Adam LR:** the AttnRes queries. ## Baseline: clean KMA Branch [`fasttrack-moe-kma`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/fasttrack-moe-kma) @ `4eba59cafa`. Build from this branch. The recipe below covers every model and optimizer component. Values are for d512 unless noted; the code is `experiments/grug/fast_track/{model,optimizer,heuristic,launch}.py`. **Shape** | Rung | Width D | Layers | Local (KDA) / global (MLA) layers | Heads × head dim | Batch | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | d512 | 512 | 6 | 4 / 2 | 4 × 128 | 128 | | d768 | 768 | 8 | 6 / 2 | 6 × 128 | 128 | | d1024 | 1024 | 12 | 9 / 3 | 8 × 128 | 256 | | d1280 | 1280 | 14 | 10 / 4 | 10 × 128 | 256 | - Every 4th layer and the last layer are global; all other layers are local. - The run uses a 16k vocab and sequence length 4096 with packed documents. Every ShortConv and the KDA state respect document boundaries (the KDA state resets at each document start). - Weights are initialized with std 0.5/√D. Compute is bf16. **Embedding and output** - Token embedding → RMSNorm → GatedNorm. The result is AttnRes source 0. - Output path: final AttnRes gate → RMSNorm → GatedNorm → untied lm_head (`output_proj`). - The fused lm_head + cross-entropy loop uses a vocab tile of 8192. - GatedNorm (every GatedNorm in the model) is `x · sigmoid(W_up · SiLU(W_down · x))`, with a rank-128 bottleneck. **Block (every layer)** - **Attention sublayer:** input = its AttnRes gate mix → RMSNorm → GatedNorm → mixer (KDA or MLA). - **MoE sublayer:** input = its AttnRes gate mix → RMSNorm → GatedNorm → MoE → ShortConv on the MoE output. - Each ShortConv is a 4-tap causal depthwise conv. **Local layers: Kimi Delta Attention** (Kimi K3's layer) - **Projections:** q/k/v are D → N·128 with full heads (no GQA). Each goes through a ShortConv followed by SiLU. q and k are L2-normalized, and q is scaled by 1/√128. - **Decay:** per-channel log-decay `g = −5·sigmoid(exp(A_log)·(x·W_a_down·W_a_up + dt_bias))`. - The gate projection has rank 128. - `A_log` is one value per head, initialized to 0. - `dt_bias` is one value per channel, initialized so the decay rate spans 0.02–0.5. - **Write strength:** `β = sigmoid(x·W_β)`, one value per head. - **Recurrence:** `S_t = (I − β·k·kᵀ)·Diag(exp(g))·S_{t−1} + β·k·vᵀ`, read out as `o_t = S_tᵀ·q_t`. - It runs as chunked Pallas kernels, with a stable block-doubling inverse inside each chunk. - **Output:** per-head RMSNorm with a learnable 128-wide scale shared across heads → full-rank per-channel gate `sigmoid(x·W_g)` → `W_o`. - No positional encoding, no window, no XSA, and no ShortConv on the branch output. **Global layers: MLA + Inkling relative position** - **q:** full-rank, D → N·128 (no Q latent). - **k and v:** k = `W_uk · RMSNorm(x·W_dkv)` and v = `W_uv · RMSNorm(x·W_dkv)`. - They share one 512-wide KV latent, with a learnable RMSNorm on the latent. - Heads are 128 wide with no RoPE part. - There's no ShortConv on K, so the up-projections can be absorbed at inference. - **Scaling:** no QK-norm; `qk_mult` = 1, i.e. standard 1/√128 logit scaling. - **Position — Inkling relative-position bias**, added to the pre-softmax logits in place of RoPE: - `bias[h,i,j] = R[i,h,:] · P[:, i−j]`, where `R = x·W_r` is 16 values per head. - `P` is a bank of shape [16 × 1024] shared across heads. The relative extent is 1024. - It runs inside the FA4 attention kernel (forward, backward, and the SM90 backward pass). - **XSA** (exclusive self-attention): subtract the component of each head's output that is parallel to its own value vector. - **Output gate:** per head, `2·sigmoid(x·W_gate)`. `W_gate` is zero-initialized, so the gate is 1 at init. - The branch output also gets a ShortConv. **MoE sublayer (LatentMoE with quantile-balanced routing)** - **Experts:** 384 routed experts, top-8. Each is a SwiGLU with hidden size D/2. - **Latent space:** experts operate in a D/2-wide latent. The input goes through `W_latent_down` → RMSNorm, and the combined expert output goes back up through `W_latent_up`. - **Router:** reads the full-width token and computes logits in fp32. - Experts are selected by top-(8+1) on bias-adjusted logits, where the 9th logit is the threshold α. - Combine weights are the sigmoid of the unbiased logits, renormalized to sum to 2.5. - **Quantile balancing:** each step, each expert's threshold β is the global (1 − K/E) quantile of the logit margins (logit − α), read from a 10k-bin histogram. The router bias is set to −β. - The router bias is not trained by gradient. - **Capacity:** capacity factor 1.15, with pooled-wave expert-parallel dispatch. Receiver ranks are sort-based and the expand backward is gather-based. - **Shared experts:** 2 shared SwiGLU experts that bypass the latent: D → D/2 hidden → D. - **Fused projections:** - The router, latent-down, and both shared experts' gate/up projections run as one GEMM. - The shared experts' down-projections run as one GEMM. **Residual stream: Block Attention Residuals** - **Sources:** the embedding source, one running sum per completed block of sublayer outputs, and the running partial sum of the current block. - The model has 8 blocks. Block sums use the raw sublayer outputs. - **Gates:** every sublayer (attention and MoE) has its own gate, and there is one final gate before the output norm. Each gate has one learned pseudo-query `q ∈ ℝᴰ`, zero-initialized so every gate starts as a uniform average. - **Mixing:** per token, `logitᵢ = q · rms_norm(sourceᵢ)`, using a parameter-free (frozen) RMS key norm, then `softmax` over sources and a weighted sum of the raw sources. - **Implementation:** - Each completed block is scored once against every gate that reads it. - Backward: at d512 the layer's forward intermediates are saved. At d768–d1280 each layer is recomputed. At d1280 the attention branch is also rematerialized. - The model keeps one layer stack per mixer kind. **Optimizer** | Group | Update rule | LR | Parameters | |---|---|---|---| | `muonh` | MuonH | MuonH LR | all attention and MoE matrices: MLA `W_q`/`W_dkv`/`W_uk`/`W_uv`/`W_o`; KDA `W_q`/`W_k`/`W_v`/`W_o`/`W_g`; experts; shared experts; latent down/up. Also every GatedNorm `W_down`/`W_up`. | | `kda_beta` | MuonH | 2 × MuonH LR | KDA `W_β` | | `adamh` | AdamH | MuonH LR | lm_head (`output_proj`) | | `adam` | Adam | Adam LR | token embedding; router; attention output gate; router bias slot (overwritten by QB); all 1-D norm gains; ShortConv kernels; KDA `W_a_down`/`W_a_up`, `A_log`, `dt_bias`; Inkling `W_r` and `P` | | `attn_res_query` | Adam | 0.1 × Adam LR | the AttnRes pseudo-queries | - **MuonH:** Nesterov momentum 0.95 → Newton–Schulz orthogonalization (5 quintic steps, bucketed across same-shape matrices) → a step along that direction, then projection back onto the matrix's Frobenius sphere. Each matrix's norm stays fixed at its init value. - **AdamH:** the Adam direction with the same Frobenius-sphere (hyperball) projection. - **Adam:** β1 0.9. Only the router and the attention output gate get decoupled weight decay (0.02). No other parameter gets weight decay, and there's no gradient clipping. - **Schedule:** 1% warmup, then linear decay to 0.05× peak. - **Peak values** from `MoeHeuristic` (they depend on tokens, width and batch): - Adam LR = `0.0876 · tokens^−0.346 · D^−0.345 · √(tokens per batch)`. - MuonH LR = 13/3 × Adam LR. - β2 = `0.999^(tokens per batch / 131072)`. - ε = `9.68e−18 · √(steps)`. - At d512 with 2384 steps: MuonH LR 0.0227, Adam LR 0.0052, β2 0.996, ε 4.7e−16. Submit (the default priority is interactive): ``` NO_PROXY="*" uv run python -m experiments.grug.fast_track.launch --submit \ --target-cluster cw-us-east-02a --priority interactive \ --run-id --size d512 --recipe kma --num-steps <8-min steps> --version ``` ## Compute - cw-us-east-02a at **interactive** priority. - **At most 10 active runs at once**, probes included. - **Limit runs above d768** to keep the experimentation rate high. d1024 and d1280 runs take hours and hold a slot the whole time, so save them for changes that have already passed gate 1 or that need extra scales because of curve-fitting risk. - Don't save checkpoints (the launcher default). ## For humans Comment with a research direction for the agent, for example "try X", or "combine A and B". The agent picks up new comments at its next batch. The main goal of a single experiment should be to learn about the system. This means that if you tweak one knob and the loss goes off the rails, the experiment can still be considered a success! We better understand the system sensitivity! Building knowledge through failed experiments will bring us closer to the long term goal of better models. ## For the agent - Read `experiments/grug/fast_track/README.md` and `agent.md` first. Where they differ from this issue, this issue wins; the main difference is the fixed-time objective. - Run 5–10 experiments per batch, and prioritize human comments when picking the next one. - Ask for clarification in the thread if helpful, but never hold a batch waiting for an answer: state your assumption and correct it in the next batch. - Start at d512. When a change beats the current best by more than 0.005, validate it at d768. - Post **one comment per batch** and edit it as runs finish. Start it with 🤖 and include: - the batch goal, and which human comments it addresses; - a table with one row per run: change | branch@commit | W&B link | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ vs current best; - a 1–3 line takeaway and the planned next batch. - **Branches:** prefix with `ladderclimb_v1_`, and link the exact commit each job ran. - **W&B:** project `marin_moe`, with short prefixed run IDs such as `lc1-b03-…` (names over 128 characters fail at init). - Add the `agent-generated` label to any issue or PR you open. - Keep the **Status** table below updated with a concise chronology of improvements. ## Studies Deep dives and multi-batch studies, newest first. Pages are claude.ai artifacts; batch comments hold the plan, every run and the numbers. | study | what it found | page | batch comments | |---|---|---|---| | **lm_head soft-cap shape** | Tanh caps 10–12 are flat on the current recipe (11: +0.0004 on 2 seeds). `A·σ((z+B)/C)` is a tanh cap `A/2` on `A/(4C)·(z+B)`, so its knobs are cap, gain and shift. At cap 11, shift ±4 and gain 0.8 / 1.25 all land within the 0.003 same-function noise; lower gain and either shift lean worse. threads.title: [grug] Resume Hero pipeline checkpoints
threads.body:
Save and resume Hero pipeline model parameters, optimizer state, and pending QB router updates through Levanter's completed `step-N` checkpoints. The stage-independent tree uses global layer paths and restores into the compiled MPMD placement, including pinned-host optimizer state; unused compiled input leaves retain their initialized placement so saved values remain representable. `--steps` remains the total training schedule length across restarts.

CPU round trips for AdamW and MuonH pass with a changed stage split; the focused Hero and original Grug pipeline tests have 16 passes and one skip. The affected safe suite has 2,198 passes, four skips, five expected failures, and eight macOS loopback failures independently reproduced on the base branch and addressed separately in #9442.

On two H100x8 nodes, a reduced-width four-layer pipeline saved step 1, restored it, and completed step 2. Resumed step-2 loss was 6.94263744 versus 6.94263697 in an uninterrupted control (absolute difference 4.77e-7). A separate two-layer, full-width Hero probe (d6144, 384 experts) at sequence length 4096 also saved step 1 and resumed through step 2. Resumed step-2 loss was 11.56717205 versus 11.56716919 in its uninterrupted control (absolute difference 2.86e-6). All six save, resume, and control jobs completed with finite losses and both Iris and native worker exits at zero. Both configurations used PP2, EP8, BF16 MuonH, and pinned-host optimizer state. Checkpoints were written only to scratch storage.

These are bounded checks; the full 48-layer, 65K-token Hero training shape has not been checkpointed and resumed. The GPU probes used the pinned JAXPP build plus local offload and DIME patches required by the Hero pipeline; durable upstream support remains a dependency of #9279. Existing Hero FSDP checkpoints have a different stacked state tree with optional master and EMA weights and are not importable by this runner. Stacked on #9279.

threads.title: [grug] Hide the ragged MoE transports under compute
threads.body:
Raise the hero step's communication/compute overlap from 60% to 81% of collective time on one rack. The ragged backend now pipelines its two expert chunks, and the model keeps small collectives out of the transports' windows. A profile-guided latency estimate lets XLA place each transport under enough compute.

The hero runs with collective overlap limited to 1, so a single collective can be in flight. Before this change, the ragged transport serialized its chunks behind a barrier, so the first dispatch and first return had no GEMM to hide under. Small collectives also took the only slot inside the MoE section: the transpose rule's two offset all-to-alls, the FSDP gathers of the latent and shared-expert weights, and the router's QB pmin/pmax/histogram reductions. XLA also rematerialized the attention weight gathers after scheduling as exposed synchronous all-gathers. Each commit removes one of these causes:

- The chunks run as a two-stage pipeline, so chunk 1's dispatch overlaps chunk 0's expert MLP and chunk 0's return overlaps chunk 1's.
- The backward takes its transfer offsets from the mirror parameters instead of exchanging them. A test checks that the two parameter sets are each other's transpose.
- The attention projections re-gather their weights for the backward at the JAX level, as ordinary async all-gathers.
- The MLP-section weights are gathered before routing, and the QB statistics run after the routed MLP. A forward-only barrier enforces both, so the gradient reduce-scatters still fuse.

The code changes alone leave overlap near 60% and slow the step by 1.3%. XLA's default estimator gives every collective the same small latency, so it hides a 3-5 ms ragged transport under one GEMM. The last commit adds `pgle_profile.py`, which turns one XProf trace into a latency profile for `--xla_gpu_pgle_profile_file_or_directory_path`. The README documents the trace, build, and rerun workflow. The profile matches instructions by name, so it is rebuilt for each program and is not committed.

Measured on one GB200 rack restored from the hero's `step-144000`, batch 1024, with production XLA flags. Overlap is kernel-classified, as in the [baseline comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8317#issuecomment-5821773936):

| | overlap | exposed collective | step |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| main (2026-09-24 baseline) | 60.5% | 1.51 s | 13.94 s |
| this branch | 60.2% | 1.55 s | 14.13 s |
| this branch + its PGLE profile | 81.0% | 0.88 s | 13.72 s |

The last row is W&B run `overlap80-v2-pgle-144k`. Its step time is 1.6% shorter than the baseline's. Loss matches the baseline to within 3e-4 at every step. Overlap is measured on one rank and depends on which: the same program and profile measure 72.5% on rank 37, whose GPU runs the step's compute 5% faster than rank 0's and spends the difference waiting inside collectives ([details](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8317#issuecomment-5860234620)). Collective busy time rises from 3.8 to 4.6 s, because a transport overlapped with a GEMM runs slower. The trace covers only rack-local collectives, and the 11-rack production program would need its own profile. The production recipe still runs without PGLE, so deploying these commits alone would slow the hero rather than speed it up.

Part of #8317

threads.title: Experiment: Hero throughput and expert drops at 8K and 16K context
threads.body:
Agent-driven experiment issue: the runs and this record were produced by a Claude agent, supervised by @mcwitt.

## TL;DR

On one GB200 NVL72 rack, restoring the hero's step-180000 checkpoint at a fixed 4.19M tokens per step, 8K context trains at 297.0k tokens/s, 1.6% below 4K, and 16K at 292.5k tokens/s, 3.1% below 4K. The fraction of expert assignments dropped rises from 1.9e-4 at 4K to 8.3e-4 at 8K (4.5×) and 2.9e-3 at 16K (16×). The drops come from the receiving shard's per-chunk capacity; the ragged transport counts all of them as `sender_dropped` (see the correction comment). Each arm has three seeds; the seed-to-seed standard deviation is at most 0.03 MFU points and 4% to 7% of the drop fraction.

## Description

The hero plan in #8435 moves from 4K to 8K sequences at 50% of training (step ~195k) and to 65K at ~95%. These runs measure what the 8K switch costs in throughput and expert-capacity drops before it happens, with 16K as the next point and a 4K control from the same checkpoint.

Setup:

* Source: `main` at f38da1173de79f1eacd5f54bcfb88db6cb0a9f6e with no code changes. Launcher: `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/launch_diagnostics.py`.
* Checkpoint: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-180000`, the newest permanent hero checkpoint on 2026-09-30. The current hero run id records that it started from step 146k.
* Hardware and parallelism: one rack (16 nodes × 4 GB200), EP64, the hero's ragged all-to-all transport and capacity factor 1.15.
* Every arm keeps 4,194,304 tokens per step (65,536 per GPU), so the learning rate from the hero's heuristic (`MoeHeuristic` in `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/heuristic.py`, which scales with tokens per step and total tokens) is the same in all arms. `--schedule-steps 390251` is the hero's full schedule length, so the restored step sits at the hero's position in the learning-rate schedule.
* `qk_mult`, the multiplier on the query-key attention scale, follows the #8435 extension rule `1.3 × (0.1 × ln(seq / 4096) + 1)`.
* Each run trains steps 180000 to 180099 with the production watch interval (10) and coordinated GC interval (100). There is no eval and no checkpoint write.
* The trainer seed sets the data shuffle, so seeds 0, 1, and 2 train on different batches.
* Statistics cover steps 180010 to 180099 (90 steps). Each run contributes its median MFU, median tokens/s, and mean drop fraction; the tables report mean ± standard deviation across the three seeds. Starting the window at step 180030 instead moves no run's median MFU by more than 0.03 points.

| Arm | `--seq-len` | `--batch-size` | `--qk-mult` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4K control | 4096 | 1024 | 1.3 |
| 8K | 8192 | 512 | 1.39 |
| 16K | 16384 | 256 | 1.48 |

Command for one run (8K, seed 0):

```bash
python -m experiments.grug.moe_hero_ep.launch_diagnostics \
  --run-id mhep-ctx8k-s0-20260930 --seed 0 \
  --num-steps 180100 --schedule-steps 390251 \
  --batch-size 512 --seq-len 8192 --qk-mult 1.39 --gc-interval 100 \
  --restore-from s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-180000 \
  --version dev --run
```

## Results

| Arm | tokens/s | vs 4K | step time | MFU | drop fraction | vs 4K |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4K | 301.9k ± 0.2k | | 13.89 s | 28.25 ± 0.02% | 1.86e-4 ± 0.08e-4 | 1× |
| 8K | 297.0k ± 0.2k | −1.6% | 14.12 s | 28.47 ± 0.02% | 8.29e-4 ± 0.39e-4 | 4.5× |
| 16K | 292.5k ± 0.3k | −3.1% | 14.34 s | 29.37 ± 0.03% | 2.94e-3 ± 0.20e-3 | 16× |

The logged `moe/receiver_drop_fraction` is zero in every run because the ragged transport hard-codes it to zero and counts receiver-capacity clipping as `sender_dropped`. Peak HBM was 103.1 GiB per GPU in every run. In every run, including the 4K control, the mean drop fraction over steps 180055 to 180099 was 0.75 to 1.00 times the mean over steps 180010 to 180054, so part of the measured drop fraction may be a transient after restore.

The live hero (11 racks, 4K) measured over steps 183310 to 183710 on 2026-09-30 had a median MFU of 26.47% and a mean drop fraction of 9.1e-5.

Caveats:

* MFU uses the analytic FLOP count, which charges more attention FLOPs per token at longer sequences (full causal attention on every fourth layer, a 2048-token window elsewhere). MFU therefore rises with sequence length while tokens/s falls. Compare arms by tokens/s.
* The one-rack 4K drop fraction is about 2× the 11-rack hero's. We have not tested the cause. The ratios between arms are the quantity to carry to the hero; an 8K hero drop fraction near 4e-4 is an extrapolation from that ratio, not a measurement.
* Each run covers 100 steps after the switch. Routing over thousands of steps at the new length is untested.
* The 8K and 16K arms change `qk_mult` together with sequence length.
* The diagnostic's peak learning rate comes from a one-rack token budget and is 0.69× the hero's. The diagnostic also leaves the attn_gate/router weight decay at 0 (the hero uses 0.02). Loss values are not comparable with the hero's.
* At 8K and 16K, XLA logged at compile time that rematerialization could only reduce its memory estimate to 193 GiB against a 161 GiB limit. The warning does not stop compilation. The runs trained normally with a runtime peak HBM of 103.1 GiB, the same as 4K, so the estimate overstated actual use.

## Links

* W&B runs (project `marin_moe`, group `moe-hero-ep`): 4K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s2-20260930); 8K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s2-20260930); 16K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s2-20260930)
* Hero plan: #8435. 262K context-parallel probe on the same hardware: #8754.

## Conclusion

At the planned 4K to 8K switch, expect about 1.6% fewer tokens per second and about 4.5× the 4K drop fraction, still below 0.1% of assignments on one rack. At 16K the costs are 3.1% and 16×.

comments.body:
> Wonder if its possible to do a clean handoff point as long as our checkpoint lands on a step that is divisible by the right number.

@ClassicLarry I've been looking into this, and it seems pretty tricky to resume with a different context length without repeating or dropping tokens. It seems like there are at least 4 independent sources of potential misalignment:

1. Levanter currently splits sources into "shuffle blocks" of 256 sequences and then the blocks are permuted. When we change the sequence length, the block sizes also change and the permuted sequence differs. So even if we restart the run at a shuffle block boundary, we'll inevitably drop and repeat tokens. #9689 fixes this by setting the tokens per shuffle block to ~1M (the current value, with 4k context), independently of the context size.
2. In addition to the block-level permutation above, we also permute _sequences_ within 512-block windows. When we change the sequence length, we change the result of permutation. (Note, we can't just work around this by doing the handoff at a step divisible by some number, since each source is at a different point in its window, and the rate at which tokens are consumed from a source is determined by its mixture weight). This seems like the largest effect after (1) and also the hardest to work around.
3. The token stream is divided into "mixture blocks" of 49152 sequences. To avoid dropping/repeating tokens, we need to hand off at a mixture block boundary. For a given batch size, mixture block boundaries coincide with steps every `49152 / gcd(49152, B)` steps. At C=16k, B=2816, this is 192 steps.
4. The data mix has a stage start at 108k. But mixture stages must fall on steps that are also mixture block boundaries, which are multiples of 192 steps at batch size 2816 (what we'd use with 16k context). We could either move the stage start to 108096 or 107904; the former skips some tokens from sources whose weight decreased at the switch and repeats some tokens from sources whose weight increased; the latter vice-versa.

One option is to merge #9689 to fix (1), hand off at the 216k permanent checkpoint to avoid (3), and accept the drops/repeats due to (2) and (4). I'm a bit hesitant, though - it seems like this has the potential to drop/repeat 10s of billions of tokens.

Wondering if we should instead look into an adhoc patch, something like finishing each source's current window in the order the 4k run was using before switching to 16k? This seems like it could get quite messy, though, and I'm hesitant to pursue it unless we think it's really necessary.

@ravwojdyla @Helw150 curious for your thoughts here as well. How did we manage this for the 67B run?

🤖 **Proposal: a clean context-length handoff** (replying to @mcwitt's four misalignment points above)

1. Fix shuffle blocks at ~1M tokens, so the level-1 block permutation is the same at every seq_len (#9689).
2. Give each data-mix stage its own `seq_len` and `batch_size`, e.g. `(216000, mix2, seq_len=16384, B=2816)`. A stage then only has to land on a mixture-block boundary in its own units, which fixes points 3 and 4.
3. Track each source's read position in **tokens** carried across stages, instead of in sequences of a single length.
4. On a `seq_len` change, advance each source to its next shuffle-window boundary (skip-to-window). Nothing repeats; only the unread rest of each source's current window is skipped, which fixes point 2. Using `harrier_mix_2026_08_18` at a 216k handoff, that is about **52B unseen tokens** across 200 sources, ≈0.26B each and ~0.6% of the remaining run.
5. Inside a stage, mixing, batching and BOS/EOS/segment handling are unchanged.

Finishing the partially read windows instead would serve leftover 4k slices glued into 16k sequences. Those need segment and loss masking at the joins, carry only 4k of context, and low-weight sources would keep serving them for thousands of steps after the switch. So skip-to-window looks like the better trade-off.

Thanks for the thorough investigation! The 67B would have had some reshuffling on its context length change, I did not account for all levels of the shuffle there.

I am in favor of skipping ahead to each data bucket's next 512-block window. So at most a data bucket will skip 512x256x4096 = 500 million tokens. I cant think of a clean way around this.

In the future a solution might be to not permute sequences in step 2, and instead only permute at max_seq_len, where max_seq_len is based on what we will eventually use in the training run.

We will face this challenge again when we go to 65k. So perhaps we should have the code permute sequences at 65k now, then chop up at 16k.
Wondering what Rav and Will think here. Would defer to them on what we think will minimize impact.

For the hero, we already shuffled the data globally in Datakit, so we could keep a fixed token-sized I/O block shuffle and drop the inner sequence shuffle. That'll make our shuffle logic context size independent for the rest of the run (and I agree skip the rest of the current block for everything here).

> For the hero, we already shuffled the data globally in Datakit, so we could keep a fixed token-sized I/O block shuffle and drop the inner sequence shuffle. That'll make our shuffle logic context size independent for the rest of the run (and I agree skip the rest of the current block for everything here).

is the only benefit of the inner shuffle to decorrelate individual batches? So if we have one very long document it doesn't end up dominating a single batch? Would we be losing this if we dropped it, if datakit shuffle is only at a document level?

Long term, we should add `seq_len` to `BatchSchedule`. For each shuffle window, shuffle at the largest context length used while consuming it, then split into smaller sequences as scheduled. With divisible lengths and transitions aligned to those larger units, this preserves data order across context changes without requiring a globally shuffled store.
The inner shuffle was mainly intended to make it so that you didn't need to globally shuffle at write time and so you can test variance from different global shuffles w/o storing write copies.

@ravwojdyla and I just chatted. I'm probs over-engineering above.

We should just skip the rest of each source's current shuffle window whenever we change `seq_len`. It's the lowest-risk option: it preserves the shuffle behavior that's been working so far, at a small cost (50B tokens worst case). Those tokens will come back around if we exhaust a bucket; otherwise, we'll use fresh tokens in their place.
Ok- so we will repeat the same procedure when we go to 65k?

threads.title: [levanter] Count full-attention layers explicitly in lm_flops_per_token
threads.body:
Count the 26-layer Snowball model's seven full-attention layers in the shared `lm_flops_per_token` estimate. The harness previously counted six, as noted in #9613, because the June trainer used a private estimator with an explicit layer-count argument. The long-layer schedule, every fourth layer plus the last, was also specified in three places.

`lm_flops_per_token` now accepts `num_full_attention_layers`, which takes precedence over the `global_every` stride. The June trainer and Snowball synthetic harness use the shared helper, and the private estimator is deleted. For the Snowball shape, the shared helper matches the deleted function exactly at 4096 and 65536 tokens. The Snowball model exposes `long_attention_layer_mask` for its scan and `num_long_attention_layers` for the harness; the June trainer counts layers with its model's existing schedule function. A test confirms that the harness and June trainer calculate the same FLOPs per example for that shape.

The corrected estimate raises the harness's measured MFU by 0.4% at a 4096-token context. The harness docstring's undercount note is removed.

Part of #9462

---

<details>
<summary>Verification: how the numbers were checked</summary>

All comparisons are exact float equality, not tolerances.

1. **Deleted June helper against the shared helper.** The private `_lm_flops_per_token` from the pre-change `experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/train.py` and the shared `lm_flops_per_token` with `num_full_attention_layers=7` were called with the Snowball shape (hidden 2560, intermediate 1280, shared 2560, 26 layers, 20 heads, 5 KV heads, 256 experts, top-4, window 2048, vocab 128256). Results: 5,305,917,440 FLOPs per token at 4096 tokens and 9,735,741,440 at 65536 tokens from both functions. The old stride path (`global_every=4`, six full layers) gives 5,284,823,040 and 9,081,815,040, the 0.4% and 7% undercounts.

2. **June trainer before and after.** `_compute_flops` from the pre-change module and from this branch were run on 36 configurations: layer counts 1 through 12, 24 through 28 and 64, each at the June default shape and at the Snowball shape. 3. **Harness against the June trainer.** `experiments/grug/snowball_synthetic/test_flops.py` builds a June config from the Snowball shape and asserts both estimators give the same FLOPs per example and seven full layers. It runs in CI.

4. **Model behaviour.** `lib/levanter/tests/test_snowball.py` (14 tests, excluding slow, checkpoint and HF cases) passes with the scan using `long_attention_layer_mask`, and the harness tiny preset trains on CPU.

threads.title: [grug] Benchmark OLMo-core kernels for incremental MoE speedups
threads.body:

threads.title: Support context-length switches in the hero run
threads.body:
Let the hero switch context length mid-run without changing its training schedule. The ladder launcher takes `--seq-len` and holds 4,194,304 tokens per rack per update, so the sequence batch shrinks as the context grows (2816 sequences at 16K on 11 racks). The step count (390251), learning rates, decay, gate/router weight decay, and `run_progress` therefore match the 4K run. A changed context requires an explicit `--qk-mult`, applied to all attention layers; `--capacity-factor` overrides the expert receiver capacity.

Harrier now shuffles blocks of 2^20 tokens (`io_block_size = 2**20 // seq_len`), which equals the existing 256-sequence block at 4K. At a longer context the outer block permutation stays the same, so only each cell's in-progress 512-block window reorders. With the previous sequence-sized blocks, a 16K relaunch would have re-read an estimated 2.85T already-seen tokens of the remaining ~9T. At 16K the past main-mixture boundary moves from step 108000 to 108096, and a continuation must pass `--accept-mixture-boundary-shift`.

Canonical hero eval stays at 4K packing, so the inherited `eval_dropless/*` series remains comparable, and the first-step eval now also runs after a checkpoint resume. Per-example FLOPs rise with context, so a FLOPs baseline (`--flops-baseline-step`, `--flops-baseline-total`) keeps `throughput/total_gflops` continuous across the handoff. `trigger_hero.sh` records the context, QK multiplier, capacity, eval context, FLOPs baseline, and boundary acceptance in the W&B lineage and the #8506 launch record. `launch_diagnostics` gains `--optimizer-tokens-per-step`, `--gate-router-weight-decay`, `--eval-seq-len`, and `--eval-prefix`, so a one-rack rehearsal can use the hero's optimizer settings and report long-context eval separately.

The live run is unchanged. A switch still needs a GPU rehearsal from the handoff checkpoint and agreed trial thresholds; see the inventory and validation plan in #9615.

threads.title: [levanter] Expose the pure-JAX flash attention to Grug as xla_flash
threads.body:
Grug attention gains an `xla_flash` implementation for AMD GPUs and any other backend without a CUDA or TPU attention kernel (#9462). It is Levanter's existing pure-JAX flash attention, which has a custom backward, called on Grug's raw arrays: KV heads are aligned, the arrays named, and Grug's causal, sliding-window and segment-id mask translated into Levanter's. The module moves from `levanter.models` to `levanter.layers`, beside the attention module that was its only caller, so the Grug layer can import it without reaching above itself. The block size is the largest power of two that divides both sequence lengths, capped at 1024, with the reference path for lengths no block of at least 16 divides. The wrapper lives in `levanter.grug.attention._xla_flash`. The Snowball synthetic harness gains an `--attention` flag that accepts every Grug attention implementation.

A scan-based blockwise draft without a custom backward was measured first on 8× MI300X with the 4-layer Snowball shape and was slower than the reference at both 4,096 and 16,384 tokens, and used more memory at 16,384 (1.38 s against 0.935 s per step, 92 against 81 GiB), because autodiff stored every key block for the backward pass. That is why the existing implementation is reused rather than a new one added. Measured the same way, `xla_flash` runs within 4% of the reference step time at both lengths (0.395 against 0.385 s at 4,096 tokens, 0.968 against 0.935 s at 16,384) and cuts peak memory from 81 to 32 GiB per GPU at 16,384 tokens, with identical loss.

threads.title: [datakit] Score quality from the tokenize stage's token ids
threads.body:
Score quality from the token ids the tokenize stage already wrote instead of
re-tokenizing text in the scoring workers, with the classifier trained on the
marin-tokenizer vocabulary. The stage reads each document's stored `input_ids`
from the tokenize attribute shards, regroups chunk rows, scores begin/middle/end
windows of `max_tokens` ids, and reads the normalize shard's text in lockstep
only for the samples side output. Label text at train and calibration time goes
through the tokenize stage's own per-record encoder, so training ids equal
stage ids byte for byte, special tokens included; a model whose meta tokenizer
differs from the tokenize artifact's is refused with the retrain command.
`train.py` now also fits the calibration, so one command produces the model
dir, and the default model dir and version tag become `pooled_junkgate2_marin`
/ `pooled-junkgate2-marin`.

Measured on the local 35k-document FineWeb-Edu set with a scorer trained on
1,500 Kimi-labeled documents, one worker, JAX on CPU:

| | text path, e5 model | token ids, marin model |
| --- | --- | --- |
| label encoding equals stage ids | n/a | 2,000 / 2,000 documents |
| holdout AUC / Spearman | 0.715 / 0.42 | 0.768 / 0.52 |
| score one shard, wall / CPU | 44.7 s / 115 CPU-s | 6.4 s / 32 CPU-s |
| peak worker memory | 3.1 GB | 1.9 GB |

Output keeps the store contract: same basename as the normalize shard, one row
per document in the same id order, samples carry text. The local full graph
(normalize, tokenize, quality, store, quality report) ran end to end on the
new stage, and on an 8-shard set a rerun after deleting three output files
rescored exactly those 13,121 documents and matched a fresh run file for file. Agreement with the e5
model on the same documents is Spearman 0.77 and 83% within one bucket; it is a
different model on a different vocabulary, reported rather than gated.

The quality step now depends on the tokenize step, so it runs after it per
source instead of alongside it, and it needs reference-pipeline tokenize
outputs at artifact v4. The default model dir does not exist yet: the retrain
on the oracle labels is one command, documented in the fast_transformer README,
and has to run before the next reference pipeline run. Windows move from 2,000
characters to 512 marin tokens, which covers about the same text for English
and code and less for CJK; the tokenizer revision pin stays identity-only.

threads.title: Pod creation fails on a node with 65K empty Silo cgroups
threads.body:
On October 2, new pods failed to start on CoreWeave node `g5bc6da`, blocking new jobs. Kubernetes reported `no space left on device` while creating a pod’s cgroup, the kernel group used to track and limit container resources. The node still reported healthy, and its filesystem had 3.55 TB free.

The host cgroup tree had 65,535 descendant groups. Of these, 65,412 were under `/silo`; that entire subtree contained no processes. This strongly suggests exhaustion of the kernel’s roughly 64K memory-cgroup ID space, though we have not traced the failing allocator.

Silo is the nested container runtime running inside our privileged Iris job `muchanem.cap-pipeline-host-53`. Two sampled container IDs from its `containerd-shim` processes matched empty `/silo` cgroups. This points to a cleanup problem in that workload’s runtime, but we have not identified the code path responsible. We have no evidence that CoreWeave’s host containerd created these groups.

Please investigate whether completed containers leave cgroups and shim processes behind, and fix the cleanup path. Verify that repeated container creation and teardown do not keep increasing either count. Coordinate cleanup of the affected node with the pipeline owner; an empty cgroup alone does not establish that it is safe to remove while the runtime is active.

---

threads.title: [marina] Host an MFU tracker with commit attribution per hardware lane
threads.body:
Nothing shows MFU per hardware over weeks or ties a change to the commits that caused it. Grafana's MFU panels group by run and span at most 7 days, and the canary regression gate (`scripts/ci/validate_canary_metrics.py`) checks only steps and loss. The TPU canary lost 7.9% MFU on 2026-09-09 (0.661% to 0.609%, tokens/s down by the same amount), and no check flagged it for three weeks. A manual bisection on 2026-10-02 put it on #8960; the procedure is in #9703.

A prototype page, built from existing data, already shows each lane on a shared date axis, flags any change larger than 3× that lane's median run-to-run movement, and lists the commits in each flagged range that touch training code, with a step-by-step bisection plan. It is a static page built by local scripts, so it goes stale and its bisection results live in one browser.

Plan: host it as a checked-in Marina app, `infra/marina/apps/mfu-tracker/`, on the EvalDash pattern.

- A scheduled `refresh` job in `app.toml` writes runs and changes into the app's Postgres schema once a day, at 18:00 UTC. The TPU canary usually starts between 10:00 and 12:30 UTC and the H100 canary between 14:00 and 17:00 UTC, so one run picks up both.
- Lanes and sources:
  - GB200 hero: W&B `marin_moe` run history, each run cut to the steps it trained before the next handoff.
  - TPU v6e-4 canary: Finelog `levanter.metrics`.
  - 8×H100 canary: W&B, because its cluster has no Finelog deployment.
- Commits: `git_commit` from the W&B run config for runs since #9637, falling back to each canary's GitHub Actions head SHA, joined on `RUN_ID`. Commit ranges and suspect commits come from the GitHub compare API, since a Cloud Run job has no checkout.
- Bisection steps and their measured MFU are stored in the app's schema, so everyone sees the same state.

Open questions:
- Which W&B key the refresh job should use, registered as a job secret the way EvalDash registers its CoreWeave keys.
- How the hero lane should find accepted deploys. They are hard-coded from #8506 today; a W&B tag or group on accepted hero runs would remove that.

Done when:
- The app is deployed behind the oa.dev login and listed on index.oa.dev.
- Each day's scheduled canary runs appear in their lanes by the next refresh, with their commits.
- A move past a lane's threshold shows the commit range and its suspect commits.
- Bisection results entered by one person are visible to others.

🤖
# Research

The [canary gate](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f0a9d853c5ef6a71d35f6b22931fd983662e4c6c/scripts/ci/validate_canary_metrics.py#L34-L38) checks steps and loss, so the reported MFU drop could pass. Marina already provides scheduled jobs, an authenticated API, and an app-owned Postgres schema; the missing pieces are durable metric ingestion, a reliable accepted-hero sequence, and commit attribution. A low-effort prior-work and duplicate-work check found no open tracker PR or duplicate issue; #9637 has merged, while the bisection procedure in #9703 is still open.

**Relevant code**
- [EvalDash manifest](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f0a9d853c5ef6a71d35f6b22931fd983662e4c6c/infra/marina/apps/evaldash/app.toml#L9-L17) — scheduled job pattern
- [Marina deploy](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f0a9d853c5ef6a71d35f6b22931fd983662e4c6c/infra/marina/__main__.py#L200-L217) — explicit job secret registration
- [Hero handoff](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f0a9d853c5ef6a71d35f6b22931fd983662e4c6c/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/trigger_hero.sh#L62-L95) — W&B parent and fork metadata
- [Hero current run](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f0a9d853c5ef6a71d35f6b22931fd983662e4c6c/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/current_run.py#L4-L6) — latest run only
- [TPU canary workflow](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f0a9d853c5ef6a71d35f6b22931fd983662e4c6c/.github/workflows/marin-canary-ferry.yaml#L30-L40) — stable `RUN_ID` and W&B project

# MFU tracker design

## Challenges

The three lanes have different metric stores. Manual canaries and hero launch attempts must not enter the scheduled or accepted baselines. A short W&B `git_commit` needs resolution to a full SHA before a GitHub compare, and older runs may have no commit. A failed source query must leave the last good timeline visible.

## Costs / Risks

Historical backfill and GitHub comparisons consume external API quota. The job adds a W&B credential and a small persistent catalog; limit initial backfill and cache compared SHA pairs. Missing source data or accepted-hero markers can delay a lane without changing the canary CI gate.

## Design

Add `infra/marina/apps/mfu-tracker/` with a Vue page, API, migrations, tests, and a dedicated hourly `refresh` job in `app.toml`. The job alone receives `WANDB_API_KEY` from a registered Secret Manager reference; the serving process reads only Postgres. Marina's existing IAP login and app directory expose `/mfu-tracker/`. Check the separate `index.oa.dev` listing during rollout and add its link if Marina discovery does not populate it.

Store `runs` keyed by lane and source run ID, including source URL, UTC interval, completed step interval, median MFU and tokens/s after the first 10% of that interval, hardware/config identity, full commit SHA, dirty flag, and provenance status. Store source cursors and last error separately. Each pass upserts complete runs and recomputes affected adjacent comparisons in one transaction; source failures keep previous rows and surface their age/error in the UI. Backfill a bounded historical window first, then revisit recent runs on each pass so late metrics are incorporated. Check the reducer against the September 9 measurements before locking it in.

Collect GB200 hero history from W&B `marin_moe`, TPU v6e-4 canary MFU from Finelog's `throughput_mfu` telemetry, and scheduled 8×H100 canaries from W&B `marin`. Match canaries to their exact GitHub Actions workflow run using the encoded `RUN_ID`; accept only scheduled, completed runs with the lane's hardware/config. For TPU, verify the Finelog `root_run_uid` to Iris job to `RUN_ID` join on two known runs before backfill; add the run ID to telemetry metadata if that join is absent. Prefer W&B `git_commit` from #9637 and resolve its short SHA uniquely; otherwise use `hero_launch_commit` for hero runs or the workflow head SHA for canaries. Show missing or dirty provenance explicitly and withhold a commit range when either endpoint is untrustworthy.

Bootstrap an audited accepted-hero run list from #8506, then apply a `mfu-accepted-hero` W&B tag to future handoffs only after cutover confirmation. Use each child's `hero_wandb_fork_from` to cap the parent at the last step it trained before handoff. Keep failed launches out of the lane. Give the tag a documented owner and update step in the hero handoff procedure.

Compute each lane's threshold from its preceding 14 comparable run changes: require five, then flag an absolute MFU move above 3× the median absolute run-to-run move. Persist the compared run IDs, observed move, baseline, threshold, and rule version so later refreshes remain explainable. For a flag with two trusted commits, use the paginated GitHub compare API; show the complete range and identify commits touching `experiments/grug/`, `lib/levanter/`, `lib/marin/`, or `lib/haliax/`. Do not silently truncate or label a missing range as attributed.

Expose three lanes on one date axis with source links, flagged ranges, candidate commits, and the #9703 bisection procedure. Persist each bisection trial's commit, run URL, MFU, tokens/s, note, author, and timestamp in the app schema through authenticated API writes. Trials are shared and remain separate from the scheduled baseline.

## Testing and rollout

Use fixture histories to test handoff clipping, exclusion of manual/failed runs, same-config pairing, short SHA resolution, missing provenance, threshold calculation, and idempotent refresh. Test shared trial writes against Postgres and the page with a Marina journey. Backfill and compare the September 9 TPU transition with the known 0.661% to 0.609% values; verify that the next scheduled TPU and H100 runs appear within an hour with their commits. Then deploy Marina and verify IAP access and the index link.

## Open questions

- Which W&B credential owner can provision a key for a job-only Secret Manager mount? Marina currently registers no W&B secret.
- Who confirms and marks accepted hero handoffs? The current run file alone cannot reconstruct earlier accepted deploys.

🤖 Not planned. The tracker will follow the standard oa.dev path from index.oa.dev/guide instead of a Marina app. It will be a static site on Cloudflare Pages behind Cloudflare Access, with a daily GitHub Actions collector like oa-impactometer's, and a small Pages Function with D1 for shared bisection results. It will live outside this repository, so nothing here needs to change.

threads.body:

Cleanup previously selected resources by a task hash shared across attempts, so it could delete a retry’s ConfigMap before its pod existed. This caused ten hero tasks to miss startup and the remaining tasks to wait for a 30-minute JAX registration timeout. Exact-name cleanup removes the active-task-hash check and keeps failed cleanup queued for the next pass. Coordinator PDBs are created before their pods so deleting an old PDB cannot leave a retry unprotected.

Disable W&B source capture in EP and FSDP hero launchers while retaining git revision metadata. This avoids scanning a changing virtual environment during tracker initialization, which caused another failed restart.

The regression test for cleanup racing with retry dispatch fails on the old code and passes with the fix. All 70 Kubernetes provider tests and 3,163 affected safe tests pass. See the [incident report](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/592) for the failure timeline.

threads.title: [grug] Raise hero single-rack MFU from 28.2% to 31.1%
threads.body:
On one GB200 NVL72 rack, these commits shorten the `moe_hero_ep` training step from 13.90 to 12.61 s (28.24% to 31.13% MFU), with loss inside the run-to-run noise of unchanged code. The last commit adds a PGLE profile builder; with a profile built from the program's own trace, the step is 12.52 s (31.37% MFU). The changes come from two campaigns: the first worked down the step's most expensive scopes, and the second benchmarked OLMo-core 3's BF16 MoE kernels against this path (#9636) and kept the leads that paid.

Each row is one single-rack run (`cw-us-east-08a`, 64 GPUs) restored from `hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k` step 180000, seed 0, 100 steps, on main's production PJRT wheel with the code's defaults. The time is the median step duration over steps 180011-180099 without the three profiled steps, and the gain is the previous row's time divided by this row's, minus one. Repeated runs of the same code differ by about 0.1%. The runs used trees from before a final round of refactors (types, helpers, comments) whose hero program lowers identically to these commits.

| Change | Commit | s/step | MFU | Gain |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| main | b4d1761ff2 | 13.899 | 28.24% | |
| Remat discounts the host-offloaded carry | 13448300c6 | 13.737 | 28.57% | +1.18% |
| Unfilled ragged transport buffers | 5a2c8d674f | 13.542 | 28.99% | +1.44% |
| Expert-side routing-weight gradient | 107a45a8e5 | 13.130 | 29.90% | +3.14% |
| Streaming Triton short convolution | 68f741af57 | 13.059 | 30.06% | +0.55% |
| SwiGLU backward in the dh GEMM epilogue | 8313e76056 | 12.943 | 30.33% | +0.89% |
| Device-side kernel availability check | 8f1f42ab14 | | | no hero change |
| Triton router top-k | 6bd939d9b4 | 12.875 | 30.49% | +0.53% |
| Token-major dispatch scatter | 15b3ea209b | 12.730 | 30.83% | +1.14% |
| Shared and chunk GEMMs under the MoE transports | bd5ce1e2e2 | 12.638 | 31.06% | +0.73% |
| Synchronous collectives without the carry offload | b3130c11c0 | | | no hero change |
| Shared-expert SwiGLU in QuACK epilogues | 561a25e66b | 12.652 | 31.03% | -0.11% |
| No routed pre-activation store under remat | 3ed6d3a39a | 12.611 | 31.13% | +0.33% |
| PGLE profile builder, run with a profile | 26d1b19ee5 | 12.515 | 31.37% | +0.77% |

The scheduling row groups three changes that do not stand alone. The MLP-section weight prefetch (from #9481) lets the first shared expert's gate/up projection run beside the first ragged dispatch, but it also moves a weight slice behind each layer's carry offload copy on the same memcpy stream, which stalls the forward for 98-152 ms/step on the production wheel. The barrier that issues the slices before the carry copy removes that stall, and costs 0.49% on a program that does not collide; at the end of the series, disabling it alone slows the step by 0.79%. The shared-expert QuACK row is negative because, after the scheduling row, the shared GEMMs are what covers the transports: the 0.18 s/step of compute it saves left 0.24 s/step more transport exposed. Removing it from the end of the series still slows the step, by 0.35% and 0.22% in two pairs, so it stays.

Changes whose gain was below about 0.3% were removed from the final tip one at a time and kept only if the tip slowed by more than 0.2% without them; a result between 0.2% and 0.4% got a second pair. That dropped a scatter-based inverse permutation (the tip was 0.04% faster without it) and a Triton bincount (0.22% and 0.10%), and kept the routed pre-activation change (0.47%) and the shared-expert QuACK change. The four rows from the unfilled transport buffers through the dh-epilogue SwiGLU backward were measured with the inverse permutation in their base and before a behavior-neutral review cleanup; without it, the last of them ran the same 12.943 s.

Numerics: the unfilled transport buffers, the top-k kernel, the dispatch scatter and the pre-activation change are bitwise. The routing-weight gradient, the dh-epilogue SwiGLU backward and the short convolution's weight gradient change at bf16 rounding; the shared-expert SwiGLU now runs on the fp32 accumulator, so the forward changes at rounding level and 0.06-0.3% of routing assignments differ downstream, as close to an fp32 reference as before; the carry barrier moves fusion boundaries. Against main over 100 steps, the final tip's loss differs by at most 3.8e-4 (2.6e-4 with the profile), against 3.3e-4 between two runs of main. Four of about 30 runs took a late upward excursion of about 1e-3 that value-identical variants also showed, so it is run-to-run nondeterminism.

Peak HBM rises from 103.1 to 123.2 GiB of a 143.75 GiB pool, mainly the 18 GiB routed MoE output that the expert-side routing-weight gradient saves; under the carry offload the launcher defaults to `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.78` and slop 105, validated on one rack only. A ragged run without the carry offload keeps XLA's default scheduler, which ignores the one-in-flight collective limit, so that configuration now runs collectives synchronously; the hero always offloads and is unaffected. PGLE needs a profile built from a trace of the exact program and mesh, so the production run needs its own before it gains the last row; automatic PGLE stays off. The memcpy-stream collision is avoided per program here; the patched PJRT wheel that gives host transfers their own streams is left for a follow-up.

This supersedes #9481: it carries that PR's mirror transpose parameters, weight prefetch and PGLE builder, and replaces its two-stage chunk pipelining with the dispatch overlap above, which with PGLE measured 12.666 s/step against 12.783 for pipelining with PGLE, the latter on a patched PJRT wheel without the copy stall (both before the kernels above and the shared-expert change). Part of #9636; the OLMo-core comparison and its adopt/defer/reject table are on that issue. Research records: `.agents/logbooks/mfu30.md` and `.agents/logbooks/olmo9636.md` on `research/mcwitt/mfu30`.
